### step-functions-activity-worker-outside

**Claim.** With Step Functions activities, a task in a state machine can be performed by a worker that runs outside of Step Functions, for example a worker program on Amazon EC2, Amazon ECS, or even a mobile device.

**Scope.** activities in Standard workflows.

### step-functions-activity-worker-polls-getactivitytask

**Claim.** An activity worker can be any application that can make an HTTP connection, hosted anywhere. When Step Functions reaches an activity task state, the workflow waits for the activity worker to poll for a task by calling GetActivityTask with the ARN of the activity.

**Write it as.** `polls Step Functions by using GetActivityTask` · `can make an HTTP connection, hosted anywhere`

**Scope.** activity workers.

> "An activity worker can be an application running on an Amazon EC2 instance, an AWS Lambda function, a mobile device: any application that can make an HTTP connection, hosted anywhere. When Step Functions reaches an activity task state, the workflow waits for an activity worker to poll for a task. An activity worker polls Step Functions by using GetActivityTask, and sending the ARN for the related activity."
> — [Learn about Activities in Step Functions](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/step-functions/latest/dg/concepts-activities.html)

**Checked.** 2026-10-15.

### step-functions-async-express-same-name-concurrent

**Claim.** For Asynchronous Express workflows, idempotency is not automatically managed: starting multiple workflows with the same name results in concurrent executions, and internal workflow state can be lost if the state machine logic is not idempotent. For Synchronous Express workflows, idempotency is also not automatically managed, and workflows don't restart if an exception occurs.

**Write it as.** `results in concurrent executions` · `Idempotency is not automatically managed`

**Scope.** Asynchronous and Synchronous Express workflows.

> "Automatically returns an idempotent response on starting an execution with the same name as a currently-running workflow. The new workflow doesn't start and an exception is thrown once the currently-running workflow is complete. | Idempotency is not automatically managed. Starting multiple workflows with the same name results in concurrent executions. Can result in loss of internal workflow state if state machine logic is not idempotent. | Idempotency is not automatically managed. Step Functions waits once an execution starts and returns the state machine's result on completion. Workflows don't restart if an exception occurs." (columns: Standard Workflows | Asynchronous Express Workflows | Synchronous Express Workflows)
> — [Choosing workflow type in Step Functions](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/step-functions/latest/dg/choosing-workflow-type.html)

**Checked.** 2026-10-15.

### step-functions-bp-lambda-transient-retry-or-catch

**Claim.** AWS Lambda can occasionally return transient 500 service errors. As a best practice, handle these in the state machine by using Retry to invoke the Lambda function again, or Catch to handle the error.

**Write it as.** `to Retry invoking your Lambda function` · `or to Catch the error`

**Scope.** Lambda invocations from Task states.

> "AWS Lambda can occasionally experience transient service errors. In this case, invoking Lambda results in a 500 error, such as ClientExecutionTimeoutException, ServiceException, AWSLambdaException, or SdkClientException. As a best practice, proactively handle these exceptions in your state machine to Retry invoking your Lambda function, or to Catch the error."
> — [Best practices for Step Functions](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/step-functions/latest/dg/sfn-best-practices.html)

### step-functions-bp-no-default-timeout-stuck-execution

**Claim.** By default, the Amazon States Language does not specify timeouts for state machine definitions. If TimeoutSeconds is not specified for an Activity or Task state, an execution can be stuck waiting for a response that will never come, so AWS recommends a reasonable timeout on each Task.

**Write it as.** `doesn't specify timeouts for state machine definitions` · `a response that will never come`

**Scope.** Task and Activity states; when TimeoutSeconds is not specified.

> "By default, the Amazon States Language doesn't specify timeouts for state machine definitions. Without an explicit timeout, Step Functions often relies solely on a response from an activity worker to know that a task is complete. If something goes wrong and the TimeoutSeconds field isn't specified for an Activity or Task state, an execution is stuck waiting for a response that will never come."
> — [Best practices for Step Functions](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/step-functions/latest/dg/sfn-best-practices.html)

> "To avoid this situation, specify a reasonable timeout when you create a Task in your state machine."
> — [Best practices for Step Functions](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/step-functions/latest/dg/sfn-best-practices.html)

**Checked.** 2026-10-15.
